title: HashMap vs LinkedHashMap vs TreeMap: ordering, performance, cache use case
shortTitle: What is the difference between HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap?
keyPoints: HashMap is unordered with O(1) get/put and is the default choice when ordering does not matter
LinkedHashMap maintains insertion order (default) or access order (LRU mode) with O(1) get/put and slight memory overhead
TreeMap maintains keys in sorted order using a Red-Black tree with O(log n) get/put and provides NavigableMap range queries
LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true and removeEldestEntry override creates an O(1) LRU cache
TreeMap requires keys to implement Comparable or a Comparator at construction; null keys are rejected
All three allow null values; HashMap and LinkedHashMap allow one null key; TreeMap does not

s1_definition.oneliner: HashMap is unordered O(1), LinkedHashMap is insertion/access-ordered O(1), and TreeMap is sorted O(log n) – each backed by a different internal structure with different ordering guarantees.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **HashMap**: hash table, no ordering, O(1) average get/put, allows one null key
- **LinkedHashMap**: extends HashMap with a doubly-linked list of entries; maintains insertion order (default) or access order (LRU mode); O(1) with slight memory overhead
- **TreeMap**: Red-Black tree, sorted by key (natural order or Comparator), O(log n) get/put, NavigableMap interface, no null keys
- Choose based on ordering needs: no order → HashMap, insertion order → LinkedHashMap, sorted → TreeMap
s1_definition.analogy: HashMap is a filing cabinet with drawers placed wherever there is space – fastest filing and retrieval, but drawers are in no particular order. LinkedHashMap is the same cabinet but with drawers chained in the order you added them – you can walk through in filing order. TreeMap is a cabinet where drawers are always alphabetically sorted – adding takes longer because you must find the right position, but you can always read A to Z.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Map implementations

  HashMap (hash table):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ {FD4001, CUR3001, SAV2001}      │  ← no ordering
  │ O(1) get/put                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  LinkedHashMap (hash table + linked list):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ CUR3001 ↔ SAV2001 ↔ FD4001     │  ← insertion order
  │ O(1) get/put                    │
  │ access-order mode → LRU cache   │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘

  TreeMap (Red-Black tree):
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │        FD4001                   │
  │       /      \                  │
  │  CUR3001    SAV2001             │  ← sorted
  │ O(log n) get/put                │
  │ NavigableMap: floor/ceiling/sub │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HashMap, LinkedHashMap, and TreeMap serve different ordering needs. HashMap is the fastest with no ordering. LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order with the same O(1) performance, and its access-order mode enables a clean O(1) LRU cache implementation. TreeMap sorts keys using a Red-Black tree and provides NavigableMap range queries at the cost of O(log n) operations.

In the National Bank of India system, Rajesh uses HashMap for the real-time balance cache because lookup speed is all that matters. He uses LinkedHashMap with access-order for the session cache, where the least recently used session is evicted when the cache reaches 10,000 entries. For the branch account report sorted by account ID, he uses TreeMap with range queries: `accounts.subMap("SAV", "SAW")` returns all savings accounts.

Remember one sentence: HashMap for speed, LinkedHashMap for insertion order and LRU caching, TreeMap for sorted keys and range queries.
